utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber bids good morning to all persons present, the representatives of the Prosecution, of the Defence, the accused, and all the staff of this courtroom. I see that Mr. Withopf would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, prior to the witness being called in, I wish to provide the Chamber -- I wish to provide Your Honours with some information in respect to the composition of the Prosecution's trial team in future. There are four distinct issues I would like to inform you about. The first one, unfortunately, Mrs. Ruth Karper, our case manager, is leaving the Tribunal. It's her last court day today. And I wish -- like to thank her, to thank her for the very good work done. I think from her work not only the Prosecution has benefitted, but also the Defence and the Trial Chamber. I'm only making reference to the variety of lists which have been provided in recent times, and Mrs. Karper certainly played a crucial role in that respect. Mrs. Karper as of tomorrow will be replaced by Mr. Andres Vatter, who will share responsibility for a limited period of time with Mr. Hasan Younis. The second change concerns Mr. Chester Stamp. You may have noticed that he since a number of days hasn't appeared in court any more. He has been reassigned to a different team. There will be a replacement in some future. The third issue: I will leave the Tribunal by end of May in order to join the International Criminal Court. What implies, that today is my last appearance before this Honourable Trial Chamber. I would appreciate if at the very end of the today's session I would be given the opportunity to say a few words. It won't take long, maybe four to five minutes. In connection with this change, I wish to inform the Trial Chamber that as of 31st of May, Mr. Daryl Mundis will be assigned responsibility and he will lead the Prosecution's team, the Prosecution's team as the lead Prosecution counsel. Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf, for telling us about the changes in the Prosecution team. For a moment I thought you were going to announce the departure of Mr. Mundis as well. But fortunately he's staying. So we take note of these multiple departures. Of course, I will give you the floor at the end of the hearing today for you to be able to tell the Court a few last words regarding your activities. We also regret that Mrs. Karper is leaving, but you tell us that she will soon be replaced by Mr. Vatter. Today we need to continue the hearing of the witness, who will be brought into the courtroom by Mr. Usher, who will be kind enough to go and fetch him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel. Are you hearing me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The cross-examination will continue, so first of all, I shall give the floor to Madam Residovic, granting her ten minutes and not more. After that, I shall give the floor to the other Defence team. In future, to avoid the extension of time, when the examination-in-chief is over, the senior legal officer of the Chamber will tell me exactly the amount of time taken by the Prosecution for their questions. We will then allot 50 per cent time more than that for the Defence. And during the cross-examination, if the Chamber feels that that limit has been -- has expired, we will stop the examination. So from now on the time will be strictly respected so that we can avoid the situation when we have to keep the witness for an additional day, though a maximum of an hour and a half had been envisaged for the cross-examination. So I give you ten minutes, and then we will move on to the next team. At 9.25, I will be stopping you. So you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel Watters.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Proceeding from your testimony yesterday, as well as the testimony you gave in the Blaskic, Kordic, and Kupreskic cases, and taking into consideration everything you told us about your personal knowledge of the situation during your tour of duty in Central Bosnia, I would like to ask you the following: Would you agree with me that it is impossible for you to confirm in absolute terms that the foreign fighters, the so-called Mujahedin, whom you never saw yourself, were during your time spent in Bosnia under the command and control of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I do believe I did see those that may have been Mujahedin in the way that they supported -- purported themselves wearing green headbands and waving green flags and the fact that they opened fire on me and it was not usual for the ABiH to open fire on UN personnel and UN vehicles, and I assume that that group that did open fire on me were Mujahedin. As to the second part of your question, I would not -- the soldiers I saw and presumed to be Mujahedin - and it is a presumption, as they were behaving in a way that was not usual for ABiH soldiers to behave towards the United Nations - they were working on the same objectives as the ABiH on the re-taking of the high ground above Busovaca coming from the direction of Zenica near a place I think called Kaonik. I cannot say from my own knowledge that they were under the command of 3rd Corps, although they were working alongside 3rd Corps and appeared to be doing the -- the same military activity as 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. Yesterday I asked you a hypothetical question referring to a number of facts which have already been admitted into evidence in this case. As you didn't answer that question fully, allow me to remind you of what I asked you about so as to ask you that question once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the basis of the evidence that has already in the file of this case, to speed up the proceedings, I have compiled a list of events that I should like to show the witness and then I will just repeat my question. So could these facts be given to the witness, Your Honours, and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, to cover these facts quickly, I will read them out once again, and they are copied from the documents. Had you known that on the 13th of June, 1993 the command of the 3rd Corps wrote to the ABiH Supreme Command to inform them of the existence of a group of foreign nationals as well as a group of local Bosnians trained by them, in this letter the command of the 3rd Corps stated that these elements were not part of the army and that they do not wish to join it, that they are conducting their operations outside of the parameters of the law, that this is damaging the reputation of the state and the army, that they are refusing to talk to him and they believe that his duty is to arrange a meeting between them and the Supreme Command. Three days later the commander of the ABiH issued an order to the commander of the 3rd Corps to send these foreign elements to Mount Igman to work with an independent unit subordinated to the Supreme Command and, in the event they refused, to show them no hospitality and possibly disarm them. That same day, during a telephone conversation between the Chief of Staff, Halilovic, and Hadzihasanovic, he -- the latter complained about this order, saying that a conflict with these foreign nationals would mean opening a third front and he tried that Halilovic send a new order in connection with the second part of the order issued earlier. At the end of August 1993, an order signed by Hadzihasanovic was not implemented because the foreign nationals were not subordinated to the 3rd Corps Command. Early in November, during a meeting with Sir Martin Garrod, the commander of the Royal Marines and at the time head of mission for the ECMM in Zenica, Hadzihasanovic explained that he was trying to solve this problem with the foreigners either by incorporating them in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or by sending them back to their countries. In early December, in a letter addressed to the commander of the British Battalion, he stated that the Mujahedin were not under the control of Mehmed Alagic, the new commander of the 3rd Corps. In February 2004 [sic], during a conversation with General Delic, the commander of the ABiH, Abu Haris, leader of the foreign nationals, said that a number of Mujahedins still refused to be under the command of the army, after which they were requested -- they were supposed to leave the country. So I come back to my question yesterday: Colonel, proceeding from these facts as being true --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a pure technical issue, and I'm sure my learned friend can explain it. But I have my doubts whether it was in February 2004. To my knowledge, General Delic was not -- is not the commander of the ABiH any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1994. I'm sorry. I apologise. It's a typing error, and I also read it out incorrectly. In February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel -- this is my last question, Mr. President. Colonel, proceeding from these events as being true, would you agree with me that they show that the Mujahedin were not elements that were under the control of the 3rd Corps and that Hadzihasanovic took reasonable and necessary steps to resolve this problem?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this evidence, I believe that to be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn now to Mr. Dixon. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Colonel Watters, I have a few questions on behalf of Mr. Kubura. There has been some discussion about the weight to be attached to the milinfosums. A final question on this issue, and that is if you could confirm that when you testified in the Kordic case in July of 1999, you said - and I will quote from the transcript; I will go through it slowly. There is a copy available if you want it. But to save time, it's probably easier if I read it out - you said: "Don't quote milinfosums as authority. The milinfosums represented what we assessed at the time and often were only the judgement of a sergeant major or a very junior captain on what they had been told on debriefing patrols. They do not necessarily represent the facts or indeed the opinion of BritBat at the time. They were an internal document for internal use. We never expected when we were producing them that they would be held at a criminal tribunal as absolute fact. Some of it is absolute fact; some of it is assessment, and some of that assessment, with hindsight, wasn't necessarily correct." Is that what you said in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: The issue of to which unit exactly the Mujahedin were attached, would you agree with me was one of great confusion for you in BritBat?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And this was primarily because you lacked the firsthand information from the ground on this question.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You have testified today that you only saw the Mujahedin or what you presumed to be the Mujahedin on one occasion; that was in mid-April, somewhere outside Zenica, when you say you were shot at by that group. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just above Kaonik on what we used to describe as the mountain road between the Lasva Valley and Zenica. It was about -- about a kilometre or maybe one and a half kilometres up the road from the -- the junction with the Lasva Valley at Kaonik. It was what I presumed to be the -- sort of the forward -- what I was convinced at the time was the forward extent on the ABiH advance in their counterattack.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But when you saw this group, there was no indication to which brigade they belonged or whether they were associated with any particular unit at all.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they were shooting at me, I wasn't making very many sort of erudite judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was aware, they were the lead elements of the ABiH advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But you never saw any insignia in -- in this situation, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that your knowledge about the 7th Brigade, which you mentioned in your testimony in chief yesterday - you referred to the 7th Brigade as one of the manoeuvre units - was largely based on secondhand information that you had obtained from the HVO, you mentioned, from the milinfosums, from your colleagues, and so on?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also in conversation with members of the ABiH as well. That's correct. We understood that the 7th Brigade didn't particularly wish to be associated with UNPROFOR or be -- or meet us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And for -- for whatever reason, you never, then, had the opportunity to meet with the commanders, including Mr. Kubura, from the 7th Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of ever meeting Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And you had no reason -- and you never did go to their headquarters in Zenica, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In Zenica, I only went to the headquarters of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You never witnessed the 7th Brigade involved in any combat operations, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally no. The only operations I was aware of that we were involved directly with what we believed were the 7th Brigade was an incident I described yesterday, where OCA Company, Major Martin Thomas, was confronted by them when they were trying to evict the Croat population from an area in Zenica..

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Once again, that is secondhand information.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You weren't there.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You're presuming it was the 7th Brigade, are you not?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going on the understanding of the commander of our "A" Company, that he believed it was. But it is -- it is secondhand information to me. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, given that this is something you've said before, that you had to take with a pinch of salt the information that you got from the HVO about what the 7th Brigade were doing and what the activities were?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It became clear that we had to take with a pinch of salt what everybody told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Including in respect of what the HVO told you about the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And indeed occasionally what the ABiH told us about their activities as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I wish you to confirm another bit of testimony from the Kordic case regarding the 7th Brigade. I will read it out again, and if you do wish to have a look at it, you can, but in the interests of time, it probably is best if I read it into the transcript. It is when you were cross-examined by Defence counsel for Mr. Kordic, and he asked you whether you were able to develop any reliable information about the 7th Muslim Brigade at the time of your tour of duty in Bosnia. And you said: "We had a wide variety of sources of information on that and many other units. As to the reliability of that information, I should think that was always subject to question, because it largely depended on the source from which we gained the information. We would evaluate the relevant merit of that information. I would probably be sticking my neck out to say that our judgement on these situations was particularly reliable. It was the best we had at the time." Is that what you said in 1999 about the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I remember saying something like that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So you would agree with me, then, today that you did not have reliable information on the internal composition and the command structure of the 7th Brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an interesting question. At the time, it was as reliable as we were able to make it and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And looking at it today?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would stick by what I said before, and that was that to -- to define "reliable" today would cast much of that, much of our understanding belief in 1993 into doubt, I suspect, as -- as since one has heard many other things from many other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You formed a belief at the time - and this is reflected in your statement and yesterday you said it was your impression at the time that the Mujahedin were concentrated in the 7th Brigade - but would you agree with me that in light of the lack of information you had at the time and the doubts about its reliability that it is quite possible that there were elements or bands, as you said yesterday, bands of foreigners not with the 7th Brigade in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia at that time, I think all things were possible, and so I'd concur that what you say was -- was also possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And it's also therefore quite possible that there were bands of foreigners fighting in areas where the 7th Brigade was not situated and not operating?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that's the case. I would pose one question: If you think about the time of year, for example, January/February, when the weather is extremely inhospitable, I'm not sure how independent bands would sustain themselves without being part of a wider infrastructure. And that, again, was our assessment then that the idea of sort of independent people wandering around in minus 10 or minus 20 degrees, they would require some form of infrastructure to sustain them and also to re-supply them with materiel, with ammunition and weapons, and we assumed that all those with a -- a cultural affiliation to either Croat or Muslim were sustained by the relevant military.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that it's quite possible that there were elements that were not associated with the 7th Brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Elements associated elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel Watters, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have just one question and maybe a follow-up question, depending on the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, good morning.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Colonel, you were shown a document by the Defence which is a compilation or some sort of summary of alleged steps Hadzihasanovic has taken between June 1993 and February 1994, obviously after your time in Central Bosnia. I wish to talk about the time you spent in Central Bosnia. And the question is as follows: Did the then-Colonel Hadzihasanovic, as commander of the ABiH 3rd Corps, did he have between February 1993 and May 1993 the military means to fight the Mujahedin, which were, as you informed the Trial Chamber yesterday, not high in numbers, did he have the military means to fight them with the aim to get rid of them?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is a very difficult question. If you think back yesterday when I talked about the physical component, the moral component, and the conceptual or intellectual component of fighting power, if I use those to analyse the ABiH at that time, I suspect that the then-Colonel Hadzihasanovic had the physical capability, but given the situation and the quite desperate situation facing the ABiH and the Muslim population in Central Bosnia, I think to have moved against, had he wished to - and I would hope he would wish to, but I would not know - had he wished to move against them, I don't believe that for there to be a schism between the Muslim peoples in Central Bosnia at that time, which I'd presume may be the third front that was alluded to yesterday, I think that would have had irrevocable -- would create irrevocable damage to the moral component of his force of the 3rd Corps, and so in -- in purely military practical terms, I think that was probably a great dilemma that would face the commander of the 3rd Corps. Had he wished to move against them, he probably was not able to at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Because of the dilemma you were just describing.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because had he moved against them, then he would have created internal divisions within his organisation with sort of Muslims fighting Muslims. It was bad enough in a civil war where the three components of Bosnia - the Serb, Muslim, and Croat - were fighting each other. To have opened another schism for there to be fighting between Muslims, albeit some were foreign fighters, some of them were also Bosnian Muslims, I think at the time would have been militarily ill-advised and the dilemma facing a military commander was in the strict terms of command as directed by the Geneva Convention. He is required to take action against any of his command who are breaking the rules or customs of war, which patently those -- some elements within the ABiH were. And his dilemma in how to deal with that was probably not something he could resolve until the situation had stabilised later in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, the Judges only have three very brief questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you said that at a given point in time you had to recover the bodies -- the remains of two British mercenaries who had been killed. Can you confirm this fact?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They were -- they were working as medics with the -- and the 3rd Corps. And I understood with the 7th Brigade. But that was only hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is hearsay. But they were medics who were part of the BH army in your opinion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my second very brief question is: Yesterday when you spoke about the equipment of the BH, about their supplies, you said that there was an air drop of weapons. Could you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In -- in Tuzla our company was based on an airfield, and regularly at night there would be air drops of supplies to the ABiH in Tuzla. And we had reports that they included the full range of materiel, rations, ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can you explain this air drop, since there was a Security Council resolution in October 1992 forbidding all planes to fly over Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the exception of humanitarian aircraft or UN mission aircraft? So how is this possible, since there should have been a form of air control? The UN resolution stated that one should ensure that the resolution was respected. So how do you explain the fact that in spite of this resolution there was an air drop of weapons?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question, sir. Equally we interdicted through Sarajevo ammunition and weapons being smuggled in container lorries and so on. I think there were activities happening at a -- at a much higher level than our own, and -- and these were being enacted without our control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last question which arises from a question put to you a minute ago by Mr. Dixon. It concerns the milinfosums. You have testified in another case that in your opinion these daily reports were not to be forwarded outside the battalion. Their purpose was not to be communicated to the outside. We have heard other witnesses testifying, and they said that these reports went to the British Ministry of Defence. They stated the contrary. What would you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I used the term "chain of command," sir, and that would include -- and I think I said "our headquarters in Kiseljak and our chain of command," which would include through our national chain of command down through Split and back to the Ministry of Defence. And they -- they represented our version of reality on that day as best we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does Defence counsel have any other questions, or the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I let you take the floor, I spent three minutes on asking questions, so you have three minutes and no more. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, these two mercenaries were killed not far from Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Konjic wasn't in the 3rd Corps's area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: BRYAN WATTERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- I didn't say they were necessarily in the 3rd Corps's area of responsibility. What I said is the rumour that we were told was they had been serving with the 7th Brigade. Whether the 7th Brigade at that stage was in the 3rd Corps's area of responsibility or not, I am not aware. I didn't say it was a fact. They were serving with the ABiH and -- and they were murdered by the soldiers that they were serving with. I mean, that is all we knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the area of Konjic. That is what you have just said. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You said Konjic. I said that is what we believed. I don't know that as fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't have any other questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no questions further for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, this concludes your hearing. Unfortunately, as I said yesterday, you were obliged to spend an additional day here. We'd like to thank you for answering the questions put to you by both parties and by the Judges. We wish you a good trip home, and we wish you all the best in the mission you are currently engaged in. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we call the next witness into the courtroom, the Prosecution told us yesterday that they intended to withdraw certain witnesses from the list, from the initial list. At the time, I said that the Defence would express its position with regard to this matter, and the Trial Chamber would render a decision subsequently. But before I let the Defence take the floor, I would appreciate it if Mr. Withopf could confirm if it was -- if it was his intention to submit a written motion to the Trial Chamber or will his request only be supported by a memorandum, which is how the Prosecution usually proceeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the purpose of the information that was provided yesterday was to inform both the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel at the earliest stage possible about the witnesses the Prosecution will call in future, and the main purpose was obviously to inform Defence counsel in order to enable them to do a proper trial preparation and to not waste their resources for preparation in respect to witnesses which are on the Prosecution's witness list but the Prosecution won't call for the reasons as outlined yesterday. Therefore, there won't be any motion following. It was information being provided to both the Trial Chamber and the Defence. There's one issue, Mr. President, Your Honours, I wish to address. There was a confusion about a name. And if I could please go into private session for this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Let me check whether you are hearing the translation of my words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution. Before I ask you to read the solemn declaration, I should like you to tell us your first and last name,.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Peter Hauenstein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me your date and place of birth and your nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 29 January, 1957. I was born in Calgary, Alberta, Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And your nationality is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Canadian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And what is your current position and rank in the Canadian Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a lieutenant colonel, and I'm Chief of Staff 41 Brigade in Calgary, Alberta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what was your position and rank in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a major in the Canadian Forces. I was seconded from the CSE into the ECMM at -- at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you testified in an international or national court of law previously about the events that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this is the first time that you are testifying. I'm going to ask you to read the solemn declaration, please, which the usher will give you. Please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the technical break, which we will have in 15 minutes, let me give you some information regarding the proceedings here, and then I shall give the floor to Madam Benjamin, who will lead the hearing. As I have said, you are a witness of the Prosecution, and first of all you will be asked to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution. At the end of that stage of the proceedings, the Defence counsel for the accused, situated to your left, will have questions for you within the framework of a cross-examination. When that stage is over, the Prosecution may have some additional questions for you. The three Judges, who are seated in front of you, may at any point in time also ask you questions, either to clarify certain answers that you may give or to fill in any gaps that may appear in the view of the Judges. As a rule, the Judges put their questions at the end of the three previous stages; that is, the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination, and the re-examination. Those would be the general guidelines regarding the proceedings. I would like to ask you to answer questions as precisely as possible. As you know, all false testimony is excluded in all the countries of the world, and in this jurisdiction false testimony is punishable. There is also a provision that is implemented in many common law and civil law countries, and that is when a witness is testifying he may refuse to answer a question if he feels that that response could be used against him. In this very exceptional case, which normally will not apply to you, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question nevertheless, but he would in that case be granted immunity, which is different from certain common law countries where immunity is granted by the prosecutor. So in very general terms that would be the general structure of this hearing. So we have a quarter of an hour left, and I'm going to give the floor now to Madam Benjamin, whom I wish to greet, as she has come back into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Colonel, you indicated to the Trial Chamber your current position and your position when you were posted in Bosnia, but could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber give us a brief synopsis of your military experience, please, and training.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I joined the Canadian Forces in 1975 right out of high school. From that point on, I went into the armoured corps of the Canadian Forces. And after completing my basic officer training, ended up as part of an armoured regiment in Calgary. From that point on, I ended up in a variety of positions within that regiment, from troop leader all the way up to squadron commander. I have under my belt at the present time some two United Nations tours and three NATO tours. Recently I've just completed a posting in the southern region of NATO at -- south of Naples and returned last summer to Calgary. I've both trained international and nationally in a number of different disciplines. More specifically within the army of the -- of the Canadian Forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Colonel, could you describe for the Trial Chamber how the teams in the ECMM were conducted and organised and how the missions were conducted.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: It was a very unique time in the Canadian Forces at that -- in 1993. They were pulling officers from across the Canadian Forces. At that particular time, there were 12 that were brought in to Ottawa. I was in fact serving in Calgary at that time. And from there I was given the mission that I would join the ECMM. It was an interesting situation because here we were as Canada not part of the EC being seconded from and through the CSE as one of the -- the nations of the CSE and that being the monitor. We initially underwent a, if I remember correctly, a two-week training course, a familiarisation course, within Ottawa, and then from there we were deployed from there into Zagreb. Once we arrived in Zagreb, the 12 Canadians were assigned areas of responsibility or missions which we would go off and do. Initially when I arrived, I moved from Zagreb into Bulgaria as a team member of the team in Bulgaria and responsible for monitoring. From there, I was then moved into FYROM, where I undertook probably one of the very first missions of the ECMM into that country. Following that, I ended up moving from FYROM, after I completed some leave, back into Zagreb, and then I was reassigned into -- into Zenica and then from Zenica, down into Gornji Vakuf. Victor 2 was the call sign of that particular organisation of which we were a team of -- of three members at that particular time. And in order to undertake the mission from the end of May till the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you state for the Trial Chamber the objectives of the mission, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: As I understood them, in those days it was one of monitoring, one of establishing the basic situation that was on the ground in those particular days, and to assist where we could anything from humanitarian to -- to the actual military situation on the ground. It was fairly open-ended on our side, as compared to UNPROFOR, which we were under a more restricted guideline.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Could you give us the exact date that you took up your position in Bosnia, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In Bosnia, I had just returned from leave, and I think it was on or about the 29th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you state for the Trial Chamber what was the situation on the ground in Bosnia upon your arrival.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: It was much different than it was in Macedonia, or FYROM, and Bulgaria. We moved -- it was interesting because we were initially supposed to move down there by helicopter. Due to the situation on the ground, we were then rerouted from Zagreb down along the coast, ferried across on a couple of the islands, and then back into Split. Once we arrived in Split, there was a pregnant pause to allow us to -- to get ourselves orientated and then eventually be picked up by the team out of Zenica. It took us about -- I believe in the neighbourhood of about eight hours or so to get in. And as we moved in from Split, you could see a -- a deterioration of the -- of buildings, of the area, and definitely looked for all intents and purposes that we were heading into a war zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Colonel, could you list for us the area of your responsibility, please. What consisted of your ...

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Once we arrived in Zenica, we were given, once again, an orientation of the ground and what we were responsible to. I went forward into Zenica with a view that I was then pushed back to Gornji Vakuf. Gornji Vakuf was the centre and to the north was Bugojno and to the south was Prozor. So if you draw a big goose egg around those three communities, that was in essence what my responsibility was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time soon after your arrival that the situation began to change in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Change from what? The interesting situation at that time for me was the fact that we'd walked right -- it appeared that we'd walked kind of right in the middle of things. I began to realise very quickly as a result of briefings and -- and my partner at the time that we had three distinct situations within that area: And I'm talking Bugojno was under one sort of a situation; Gornji Vakuf another; and Prozor yet -- yet a third. And if you are asking me specifically about one -- one of those three communities, I tell you that each one was different.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And the question is: Could you describe them for us, please, briefly. What was the situation in Bugojno? What was it in Gornji Vakuf? And what was it in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Okay. Down -- I'll start from south and go -- going north. First of all was Prozor. Prozor was Croat-occupied at the time. There were some Muslims in that location. It was definitely controlled by the Croats. As we moved further north and through the Makljen checkpoint and moving to Gornji Vakuf, there was actually a front line in Gornji Vakuf which was clearly defined by the east-west routes downtown of Gornji Vakuf, the major community there. There is an appearance that the Croats were in the northern half of that town and the Muslims were in the southern half. It was -- Gornji Vakuf was definitely a -- an affected area, and I'm talk specifically about the conditions of buildings and -- and there were actually defensive positions within the town that were occupied by both sides. However, when we initially arrived, there was no fighting between the two sides in Gornji Vakuf. However, there had been major battles in that area, no doubt in my mind because of the conditions of the buildings. Everything was shot out and the -- the line between the two -- the two opposing sides were well defended with a number of sandbags, logs, that sort of stuff like that. As you went further north, there was a -- an appearance of a calm that existed. When we went into Prozor -- correction, into Gornji Vakuf and up into Bugojno, there was a -- it was not as damaged. There appeared to be damage on the side of -- of the road, the major road that connected the two -- the two communities, but it appeared - and I use an English expression - "the eye of the storm." There -- people looked like they were getting along. There was not much damage to the infrastructure of the town itself and the town was relatively in good order at that -- in those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Could you describe for the Trial Chamber what would have been your normal daily routine on your assignment. What did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I'll start in fact from the -- from normally the night before, and that consisted of actually reporting the day's activities to our higher headquarters, which was Zenica, and then from -- as well as all those surrounding teams around us. And I'm talking in -- up in -- or down in Mostar, Tomislavgrad, and the one up to the north. I'm trying to remember the community. It's escaped me. But anyways, basically a shotgun blast to everybody around our area of what had happened. Then we would plan the next day's activities based on our relationship with UNPROFOR in that -- in that location, which was a company of -- of infantry which were equipped with Warrior vehicles, understanding their major responsibility in those days of UNPROFOR was basically to keep the roads open and bringing in supplies straight into -- into Sarajevo, which is slightly different than what we were up against. So the night before we would plan all the next day's activities. So with that in mind, the next day we would start off, and we would commence our activities by basically visiting one of the three major communities. We would try to at least hit two of them in any given day, but depending on what meetings we had ongoing or meetings we had arranged at different levels, we would orientate our day accordingly. Initially we would be going and moving throughout the area under our own control. We were equipped with a vehicle, Land Rover with no particular protection device on it or elements on it. As time progressed, that changed, of course. But most of that time was just spent interacting with the local community and trying to determine what was basically up with every community.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, that was going to be my very next question. I was about to ask you how did you obtain the information for your reports. What did you do? Who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That was kind of a combination of -- I believe the complete chain, if you would call it that. It was everything from how we observed things on the ground personally between myself and my partner and -- what we had gathered or talked with -- with UNPROFOR who were in the location with us. Obviously we could not be the eyes and the ears everywhere, but we -- and we were only one team in that location and that responsibility of those three communities. So it was for all intents and purposes a variety of -- of sources, everything from the soldier manning the checkpoint on the ground and interaction with that particular individual to the civilian authorities in all three areas, to the military commanders in the three areas, and basically anybody we could get -- get to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would this include civilians themselves?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely. And included members of the church, both Muslim and Christian.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 10.30. We will have a break of 25 minutes and we will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Benjamin, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Colonel, before the break, we basically did a general overview of what takes place or what took place in your tenure. Now could we go into specific areas, specific periods as to what transpired. I wish to start with -- from the very beginning. Probably the first two weeks in June or thereabouts. Could you tell us what transpired in your meetings and anything of significance, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: What struck me when I first entered the AOR or the area of operation that I was responsible for was, as I stated earlier, the differences between the three communities in which we were responsible for. There were three distinct situations that were ongoing. Each appeared from our level to be autonomous organisations or ongoing situations, realising that the distance between the communities was somewhere in the neighbourhood of 35 kilometres between Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf and then an additional 35 from Gornji Vakuf down to Prozor. Because of the lay of the land, there was a distinct valley which flowed from the north down through to the south and then to the area of Prozor, which was in a very deep portion of the valley. Once again, it was -- I was struck by this whole -- beside the lay of the land, this whole different situation which was in the three communities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Would you be able to assist the Trial Chamber as to whom did you meet with? Do you -- could you tell us the -- the different representatives of the different organisations, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: It depended where we -- where we were. It varied from each community. I suspect that the area that you want to concentrate on is in the area of Bugojno. And initially, our -- my contacts there were at the -- for all intents and purposes, at the civilian governmental level in Bugojno. When I arrived, it appeared that everything was in order. Discussions were ongoing between all the local hierarchy on things like determining how to get stable electricity. I believe there was a water pump situation in the town at the time when I first arrived. They were talking about getting parts from outside of Bugojno. There was the situation and discussion about resettlement of those that had left the area before. And even to our surprise in Bugojno there was a discovery of a Serb -- a small Serb community, which was a surprise to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And that would have been the gist of the initial meetings.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: As time passed and you would have started your investigations, let us move basically towards the end of June, around the 18th of June or thereabouts. Did you meet with representatives of the different military units? And could you give us their names, you know, who was in charge and who you met with and basically what transpired during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to object to this question. The witness mentioned their observations, their information, and their meetings. My learned colleague is referring to certain investigations. As far as I can see, the witness has never mentioned any investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I think it might be a matter of interpretation. I think the witness may have alluded to the fact that part of his role as observations, speaking to people, getting informed, and that is what I referred to when I asked him in the process of carrying out his investigations. Maybe -- maybe my friend would prefer if I ask him in the process of what he spoke about. But maybe I can phrase it differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Colonel, in your daily meetings, could you indicate with us who you met with, the individual personnel, and what transpired at the meeting and what were the discussions. And you originally -- you first told us of the first set of meetings when you first got in with respect to discussions on the water situation and so. Did the meetings have any other discussions? And could we start now from around the end of June or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just backtrack a little bit on -- on the initial meetings. There was a joint organisation or committee that was in fact chaired by a gentleman by the name of Pierre Thebault, who was the ECMM representative and head out of Zenica. And he actually came down to our area. Once again, I was actually new to the area. And he actually chaired this meeting between the military representatives of Bugojno. And in those meetings, we in fact discussed, as I've already stated, it was general running of -- of the town and how -- how the situation was in general. Both sides were very cordial to one another in those meetings, so much so that it was -- these meetings were held in each of the other's headquarters in which they were then brought together, and the side that was hosting the meeting was in fact providing lunch and it was an open part of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I need to make myself a little clearer. Colonel, you said both sides were cordial in the meeting. Could you tell us who was a representative and of which sides and whom are you speaking of.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I'm referring to the -- the Croat and the Muslim hierarchy, military commanders in Bugojno. Names specifically of them are vague at this particular time, unless I would refer to -- to notes. The one that jumps to my mind is -- I believe -- no, I'd only be guessing, and to go after these names, unless you started mentioning to me who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Suffice it to say that you met with the commanders of the different armies.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Let us move --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Not of the armies. Of the operational zones in which they were responsible for. And I suspected in my area it was up to divisional commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you cannot recall the names.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I'd be searching right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let us -- did there come a time when relations in Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf -- did there come a time when things began to get tense? Did there come a time?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: To me -- once again, it was the eye of the storm in those days when I initially had arrived. There was always discussions ongoing about areas outside of -- out of Bugojno, and particularly in the area of Gornji Vakuf, of which there were problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So could you tell us what type of problems there were and what did the discussions centre around and what you saw.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In Bugojno or Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Let's start with Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Okay. In Gornji Vakuf, there -- there was always a friction between the Muslims and -- and the Croats, in that location. It -- when we did bring both sides together, they were brought together on neutral ground, being that the UNPROFOR company headquarters in the warehouse at Gornji Vakuf. Rarely were -- did we in fact take one side to the other. Excuse me. The -- the impression I got in most of those meetings -- and by the way, there appeared to be no civilian hierarchy in that location. It was meeting with the military commanders all the time. The situation in Gornji Vakuf was tense. Discussions were always around trucks disappearing, people being hijacked, information about a list of people who had gone missing in the area and general shooting incidents during the night, that sort of stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You personally while in the field, what did you observe about the area of Gornji Vakuf, the physical conditions in Gornji Vakuf? What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: To put it in the simplest terms, Gornji Vakuf was a war zone. Almost every building in that town was damaged in one form or another. There was, as I had stated earlier, distinctive defensive positions inside that town. And even when I had arrived, it was relatively calm but there was -- people were very cautious. There were -- a majority of the people walking around inside that town were -- were wearing a uniform of one shape or form or another.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: At the end of June and towards the middle of July you were on leave from your AOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell the Trial Chamber when you returned to your AOR.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The exact date? Is that what you're looking for?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Approximately. Beginning, mid, end, and of what month.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: It was -- it was July. I think it was mid-July, if I'm not mistaken. And I returned after going home for a couple of weeks' leave. And when I arrived back, the situation in the north had completely changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you relate to us what were your observations on your return to your AOR.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The day I arrived back, my partner informed me that the situation in Bugojno had deteriorated. I was -- I was somewhat upset because here I'd gone away on leave and I come back and found out that the eye of the storm had completely fallen apart. I -- after conferring with my partner, we then headed north to try and figure out what exactly had happened. My partner explained to me -- and it was a new partner, by the way, because when I had gone away, my previous partner was about to leave the mission, and so in fact when I did return I had a new partner and he -- and he'd left. This new partner and I, with relatively the same backgrounds, he explained to me how literally that things had deteriorated in Bugojno to the point where there was actually fighting ongoing inside the town itself. We proceeded north, and what struck me particularly about going north is how it had literally turned into a war zone as well. From the aspect that -- that buildings were on fire and people were -- were moving in directions. I presumed at that time Muslims were moving north and Croats were moving south.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: How did the inhabitants of the villages appear to you?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The inhabitants appeared somewhat frightened. I remember particularly several groups of people approaching us and asking us what -- what was going on and what -- what had happened. As we went into the town of -- of Bugojno, it was an eerie silence at that time, and we were in fact moving to a place, if I remember correctly, called the Kalin Hotel, which was a casualty collection point for the -- for the Croats in Bugojno. My partner had explained to me that there had been a battle centred around that hotel. And even when I was there, you could see the -- the extreme damage that had been done to that hotel as a result of fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What would be the basic ethnic composition of the inhabitants of the villages of your AOR?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In the north, when we initially started, it was Muslim and Croat with that small majority of -- of Serb. By the time I had returned from leave, in Bugojno it appeared to me that there was little Croat left in Bugojno. The number that we were able to determine was probably, I would suggest, somewhere in the four or 5.000 mark. However, we were also informed and had witnessed that there was some 10.000 that had been moving south from Bugojno down toward Gornji Vakuf. Later on in that week I believe we actually married up with some of those in -- in a town between Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno, of which we went in with a battle bus -- and this battle bus I'll describe as a bus with the capability of carrying some 35 stretchers. The bus was armoured in that it had armoured plating all around it, and it was in fact belonging to the Croats and we managed to get our hands on it, and we moved casualties from both sides back and forth. What was unique about that particular day was the fact that we arrived in -- in the area between Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno and finding that a very large group of Croats - and I'm guesstimating in the thousands anyways - were around this area, and more specifically was our problem of -- and the agreement that we had made was that we were going to evacuate casualties. We took out as many as we could with a view that we were going to be back the next day. We -- when we did come back the next day -- and by -- during all this time there is in fact active fighting going on, and there's lots of artillery -- mortar being fired from the direction of Bugojno down into this area. We managed to extract a couple bus loads of people. But what I'm leading to is the next day we ended up in a situation where we went back for them and they were gone. We believed at that particular time that Croats had in fact gone to the west into the Serb area and then migrated south toward Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. As a result of -- of what you would have seen on your return on the 24th and 25th, thereabouts, did you schedule a meeting with any of the parties?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: We tried to get into the operational zone commander. In those days -- and for the life of me, I'm sorry, I can just cannot remember the exact timing, the exact day. But there was a series of meetings and it was a mixture of everybody meeting from the operational zone commander to his Chief of Staff to the brigade commander of the day of trying to determine what had happened up in Bugojno. There were all sorts of allegations during those days of who was doing what to whom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. During this particular meeting, was anything revealed to you with respect to where the -- the inhabitants may be and -- and the casualties and things like that?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: What I can remember of the time frame, there was a basic -- they revealed that the Croats -- a lot of the Croats had left town. It was revealed that strangely enough as this battle was going on there was still a strong indication that they wanted not to fight and they in fact wanted to live together, even at this critical time, when it appeared that the Croats had been taken out of town or pushed out of town to the south. Through these meetings, we also established that there were in fact men being held in some sort of facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you eventually find out where these -- where this facility was and if in fact there was more than one, and did you pay a visit -- did you pay any visits?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Initially -- initially there was -- it was indicated to us that there was some three facilities. We had an opportunity to visit three of them over, I think, a two-day period, and we gathered as much information as we could on that situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So you had the opportunity to visit three facilities.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us who was in charge of these facilities?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: There was an appearance initially that the facilities were in charge of the local -- I'm going to say police organisation. As we went through the -- the following days and weeks, I think it became established that there was some sort of move taking place between the local authorities and being passed over to the military authorities and the consolidation of the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And which military authority would you be referring to?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I am referring to the -- the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you give us the names of the facilities that you visited?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the actual Serbo-Croat names are -- are unfamiliar to me, but I'll refer to them as the way we tended to do, and that was --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: One was a gym or elementary school. Another one was a -- a furniture salon or discotheque. I wasn't quite sure what it actually undertook. And the third one was a soccer stadium. In fact, the same soccer stadium the day I arrived in -- in Bugojno we actually witnessed a soccer game between the Brits and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So could we do them individually now. Could we start with the gym, please. Could you describe the conditions, what you had seen at the gym, if you had spoken to anybody, what you heard, and what you discovered from your visit.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: We were escorted -- first of all, like I stated, we -- it was divulged to us that they were holding prisoners. We were escorted by the local police to that facility. What struck me was -- was in kind of the middle of town there was one entrance, at the front end. There was -- beside the military police, there was my partner, my interpreter, and myself who were actually allowed to enter the facility. What struck me was, if I remember correctly, a narrow corridor which then led to an open courtyard and then the courtyard then led into the gymnasium in the back. The prisoners, as I'll refer to them, were scattered throughout the facility. Most were sitting, smoking cigarettes, and basically in -- in small groups of three or four. It appeared that they were healthy and well treated from the perspective of I assumed that they were recent captives -- recently captured. We attempted -- without any restriction, we were allowed to talk to these individuals. I remember working through my interpreter and basically, you know, asking how things were and was there anything that they -- you know, that they required. The response I got from them was, "No, no." They were more concerned about their families and what was happening with them and were generally just trying to find out general sort of conditions on the outside. Upon entering that facility, I remember distinctly the -- the large amount of women and children on the outside of that building, and it appears most had hampers of some sort in order to try to bring in. I wasn't really paying attention as to whether they were restricted or not, but were consistently -- you know, there were people kind of rotating through and trying to visit people inside that facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What about the physical conditions at the facility? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: It was an older building, obviously from probably the eighteenth century, I would suspect, if I remember correctly. There appeared to be sufficient toilet facilities, that sort of stuff like that. Most of the prisoners that I did observe were on some sort of blankets. And -- yeah, and there appeared to be enough room for the amount of detainees that were in that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Approximately how many prisoners would you say?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: From what I can remember -- I'm guesstimating somewhere between 100, 150, somewhere in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you -- were you able to observe the ethnic background of the guards at the facility?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yeah. There was no doubt in my mind that they were -- they were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And the next facility would have been the furniture salon. Could you tell us of your visit to the furniture salon.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I was -- I was puzzled by why the prisoners were kind of spread out like this. I can remember asking that specific question. They said basically they did not have a facility to hold all of the -- the prisoners, so that's why they tended to be in these -- the three locations initially. So the next facility we did go up to was -- it was a building in the middle of an open area, flat top, white in colour, and two storeys. And what I mean by that, there was an upper storey, an upper level, and then there was an lower level. And you entered kind of a flight of stairs, about four or five steps to go up into the upside, or the upper level, and then another four or five to go down underneath to the basement area. When we entered there, we were initially shuffled into the upper level. What struck me about the upper level was nobody was in there except a bunch of the guards around a small table actually drinking coffee, having a cigarette, things like that. The rest of the furniture -- it was empty. There was nothing else in this facility, and it was kind of all glass all the way around, if I remember correctly. I asked where the prisoners were, and they said, "Well, they're downstairs." And at that point in time I was allowed to go downstairs and visit them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what you observed when you went downstairs.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The conditions in that facility were much different than the elementary school. It was completely black down in the basement. There was no floor that I can remember. In fact, there were puddles of water throughout the whole facility. There appeared to be small alcoves as you walked kind of in a U underneath the ground, and each of these alcoves were occupied by groups of men who were on the ground and equipped with blankets, a few blankets. I remember the -- specifically the heat and the stuffiness. There was no ventilation in the area whatsoever. There was only one entrance and one exit from that location. It was guarded at the front end by three or four BiH soldiers. We attempted to segregate ourselves from our -- our escorts, and I -- I used my interpreter to try to find out what was going on. They were -- the appearance I got was they were -- they were very scared. There was consistent darting of the eyes back and forth between myself, my interpreter, and the guards over our shoulders. I basically asked questions, you know, "How are things going? How's the family? Do you know where you're going?" And it was very -- yes and no answers I was getting from them. There was -- and I can't remember who divulged this information, whether I got it from one of the prisoners or -- I actually asked one of the guards, and I said, "You know, have you had any problems?" And I remember specifically them telling me about a prisoner who had tried to escape the night before that they had shot. Otherwise, they'd had no problems inside that headquarters -- or sorry, that -- that particular facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What about the detainees? Would you be able to assist us with how many -- approximately how many people were held in this basement?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yeah. I -- once again, I think it's in the neighbourhood of -- of maybe no more than 100 or so. But it was -- what struck me was how crowded it was underneath and specifically how small this facility was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you get an opportunity to speak to any of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us some of ...

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Well, as I explained earlier, it was a very reluctant -- first of all, to establish who we were, why we were there, and this impression I got that they were in fear because of what they were telling us. I can't tell you specifically that they -- they, you know, passed me any particular information, but it was just the impression I was getting at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And the furniture salon, the next -- the next detention centre would have been the elementary school, as you indicated?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: No. It would have been moved from --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The stadium.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: From that over to the stadium, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Now, this was the local soccer stadium of the -- of Bugojno. Underneath the seating of the -- I want to say the north side of the stadium was a set of rooms underneath the -- the seats. These rooms were interconnected by a corridor of which at one end, at the far end, was, I believe, the washroom facilities, but on the left-hand side, as you looked at it, it was the one entrance. And what I suspect was being used as a sports facility, in fact, it would have been team rooms that were underneath the -- the seating. We -- once again, one entrance, and many guards around the outside. Each of these rooms contained, I would suspect, probably around 15 to 20 people. What struck me also about this place is how stuffy it was. There was no circulation of any air. There was some windows up on the top, if I remember correctly, but it was extremely hot and warm inside that facility. I made special note of it and even asked the guard commander. I said, "How often do you let out your people?" And they said about twice a day. And they in fact allowed them to go onto the sports field and in fact keep them contained on the sports field, and then from there they move them back into the -- into the enclosed area underneath the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What is your overall opinion with respect to the conditions of the three facilities? Would you say that it complied with the requirements under the Geneva Conventions? Were they facilities that were good for holding people, detention centres?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: If you ask me to put them in a -- a best-to-worst facility, the best was the elementary school, followed by the sports stadium, followed by the furniture salon. I accepted that these individuals had been recently captured and that there was a move afoot to move them to a consolidated facility which would be able to house this number and take care of this number. Realising that these individuals had been captured probably over a one-week period and therefore was -- as I stated, I accepted that it was a temporary facility. I was -- I made special note of bringing up the point that I felt in my professional opinion that the facility at the salon was the one that had to be dealt with fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you meet with any of the religious clergy at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Because of the deterioration of the situation, it was -- we were very quickly cut off from the hierarchy of the military of both sides and understandably so. A battle is on. The commander's responsibility is in a lot of different areas than worrying about ECMM monitors. My partner and I, we came up with a plan to -- if we couldn't get at the military commanders, then we'd try something unique and we'd start talking to what we believed at that particular time a -- the one institution that would -- we thought would remain intact, and that was that of the -- of the church and the mosque. So in Gornji Vakuf -- sorry, in Prozor and Gornji Vakuf we actually started negotiation and discussions with the local -- the local clergy. Specifically in Bugojno we hooked up with the -- the Catholic church there and a gentleman by the name of Father Janko was the person we dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And in the subsequent days to come, would you have had meetings with Father Janko?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Many.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Once again, it was a situation where the -- the Croats had become the minority in -- in Bugojno and we were trying to determine how many people were left. The guidance that we gave to Father Janko at the time was to, you know, find out who was left, gather lists of people that were still in the area, find out about food distribution and how they were going to be supported, and -- and more importantly we -- at this point in time we started to hear rumours of atrocities such as rape and killing.
