utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you have any reason to visit hospitals during your tenure? And could you tell us what you observed and ...

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Once again, it was a situation where we went after the areas where we felt we could do the most good. Besides the hospitals -- sorry, besides the church, we also started an exchange programme of injured between the both sides. Once again, we drew on that battle bus from the HVO which was -- was able to carry up to 35 litters at one time. And we used that bus to arrange exchanges and, more importantly, negotiate exchanges between the two sides. We would recover individuals out of one side, i.e., down in the area of Gornji Vakuf and Prozor. We would move them north. I'm talking we would move Muslims north, drop them off, and we would then pick up Croats and then move them south. In one particular case, we managed to recover -- UNPROFOR managed to find a group of people being held in a Croat area and which they were -- we negotiated that we be able to get them released. We brought them to the -- to the Muslim hospital in Bugojno, at which time we dropped them off. We then found out that there was some Croat soldiers being held upstairs in the hospital. We went and talked to the doctor in charge, if I remember correctly, and to say, "Can we go talk to them?" We were not restricted in any shape or any form. We went upstairs, and if -- I'm saying in the neighbourhood of about 20 soldiers, Croat soldiers are being held under guard in a room in the back. We proceeded to talk to them, and it was a mixture of, in our mind, people who had been injured as a result of battle and others who had been injured as a result of other means. We -- once again, we were peppered with many questions about what was happening, and we -- I managed to put on the table that it was an opportunity for them to leave this area if they wished.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. May I interrupt you, Colonel. You said there was some that might have been injured according to battle and by other means. Could you tell us what other means you're referring to, and how did these people look to you physically.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: It was at this point in time that some stories started coming out about the furniture salon. Some of these individuals claimed to have been beaten in that facility, and even to the point where one of the -- where we found out that the individual that may have been shot as a result of trying to escape had not been shot trying to escape but had been beaten to death.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you say that some of them claimed to have been beaten now. How did they look to you physically? What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That they had been beaten. No doubt. They showed me bruises throughout their body and even to their face of which -- there was no cuts that I can remember, but as though somebody had taken a blunt instrument and had actually struck them or with -- with a closed fist. I'm not a medical doctor, so I can't tell you exactly, you know, what injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That will be sufficient. Thank you. You are about to wind now -- you're about to wind down your tenure in your area of responsibility, and your final days would be basically meetings with the clergy and with both sides. Could you tell us what transpired to the end of the tenure and what in fact did you put in place.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: We tried to -- once again to stabilise the situation. I learned -- had learned very quickly that if the sides were going to fight, they were going to fight, and there was nothing that I as ECMM or UNPROFOR could do anything about. So once again, it was the situation of us trying to interject where we could do -- where we thought was the most good. The things that we got involved in were the exchange of prisoners of war, of the injured, of those we could get our hands on, and continuously trying to meet with the upper echelon in the military. As far as I can remember, in those last weeks we could -- I could not get a meeting with the operational zone commander. I got it with his Chief of Staff, and in fact the location had changed from the normal place we would meet to another location. It was divulged at that particular time -- and once again, we were consistently asking about the prisoners of war and where they were located and how they were housed. It was of such concern to me that I had passed it up through my chain and I was attempting constantly to get the ICRC involved, which is their job, to do this particular organisation. What came to light was that there was a fourth camp someplace. I did not know where that location was. I personally did not get to that camp before things had ended, my tour had ended. There was talk about the -- consistent talk about the consolidation of those four locations into a new location which was somewhere to the north-east, and for the life of me, I'm sorry, I cannot remember the name of the place. And it was some 30, 40 kilometres to the north-east, of which they were planning to build a new facility for -- to house these prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Colonel, during your tenure in Bugojno and the other villages which consisted of your AOR, in your opinion which army would you say was the aggressor? Which army had control? Which army played the dominant role in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: If -- if you're talking from the north -- and in those days -- it was interesting, because when I first arrived, we had always heard rumours about something not right up north. And remember, Bugojno was -- was a situation where we had what we understood on the ground that the Muslims and Croats had defensive positions up against the Serbs. To the north of that, even further, up into Travnik, during the middle of -- of my tour things began to deteriorate, and it was almost like a wave from the north as time progressed that was kind of rolling down the valley over a one-month period. I had made a -- a military guess that the Muslims were in fact going for the Makljen checkpoint, which is the top of Prozor. The lay of the land allowed that if the Muslims ever got the Makljen checkpoint they would have domination of that complete area, as Prozor was in the valley. But as the battle progressed, down from the north into Bugojno and then further south, there was a counter-reaction by the -- by the Croats, and we could see many resources being moved in from both sides in order to counter that. And what I'm referring to as -- as the Muslims move further down south, then more and more Croats were being brought in from areas such as Tomislavgrad and other places to the south of that to reinforce, as well as up north there was more troops than we had ever seen in Bugojno before. Some of these troops were not of that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] But generally, which would have been the more organised army? Which would have been the -- the one that was totally in control, so to speak, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In my military -- my professional military opinion, there is no doubt in my mind that the Armija were the better of the armies in that area at that particular time. Once again, an English expression, "the Croats were caught with their pants down."

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The bulk of the detainees that you had seen and prisoners and injured people, could you tell us what their ethnic origin would have been?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In what location?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The whole area -- your whole area of responsibility generally.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Well, it depended where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you want to divide it in three?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Let's go to Gornji.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Gornji Vakuf -- oh, boy. The Gornji Vakuf ended up the front of the line, for all intents and purposes. There were soldiers there. There was battles around the -- our area. In fact, where -- where we were permanently quartered. The battles moved around us. The Muslims in fact attacked around our warehouse to take out the headquarters warehouse behind our location in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So they were defeated in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: They were being defeated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And my question is: The POWs that you would have dealt with and perhaps the injured civilians, of what ethnic composition basically were they?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I think, once again, it depends where I was. I mean, up in Bugojno we saw, you know -- we saw every different nationality that was injured. There was a tendency to group them into -- you know, like I said, as an example, the prisoners of war or the -- the soldiers that we came upon in the hospital had been segregated from the normal population that were injured. And there was -- there was -- it was right across the whole gambit of children, women, and men that were injured. To say that -- you know, to make an identifiable mark what ethnic background, I can't give you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What about the -- the people who were forced or who left the area? What -- who basically would have left the area, the ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yeah. As we were moving -- as the Muslims were moving down to the south, they were forcing Croats to the south and -- to the point where I saw a mass exodus out of Prozor of -- of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Benjamin. For the cross-examination, I shall give the floor to the Defence, and I wish to indicate that the Prosecution took 1 hour and a quarter, so the Defence will have 50 per cent more than that, which makes it two hours. Two hours of examination. So it's quite possible that we will have to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel Hauenstein. My name is Edina Residovic, and I am representing General Hadzihasanovic. Colonel Hauenstein, is it correct to say that you gave two statements to the OTP of the International Tribunal, on the 9th and 10th of October and on the 28th of November, 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina to join the Monitoring Mission of the European Union, you first went to Zenica, where the EEC [as interpreted] mission was headquartered, headed by Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault, and he assigned you to team V2 in Gornji Vakuf; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You arrived in Gornji Vakuf on the 29th of May escorted by an UNPROFOR unit.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in Gornji Vakuf, you immediately noted that there were certain problems, because you witnessed the HVO having captured three vehicles of a humanitarian convoy, that they tried to loot it, and UNPROFOR had to intervene; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Gornji Vakuf, you learnt from your colleagues in the mission and from representatives of the British Battalion, which was also stationed in Gornji Vakuf, about the situation in the region about which you didn't have much information previously; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As part of your monitoring mission, as you have already stated, you met many leaders from the military and civilian life and other public figures who were important for the population and the community as a whole; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You never met with the commander of the 3rd Corps, General Hadzihasanovic, nor did you send any information to him about what you learnt in the course of your mission in Gornji Vakuf; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I never met the general; however -- and I would have not been required to report to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that your area of responsibility was the area of Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, and Bugojno. You knew that Prozor was fully under the control of the HVO; Bugojno -- in Bugojno, the HVO and the BH army had quite good relations; whereas, in Gornji Vakuf these two armies were in open conflict. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the OTP, you said that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a provisional army consisting partly of soldiers and partly of civilians and that - and I am adding this myself; you didn't say this - but you were able to see that this was an army that was in the process of formation. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I would say that there was a -- degrees of professionalism in that army. And why I make that statement is that I was -- I would suspect that many of the appointments within the -- within Bugojno related to the BiH was a direct result of previous experience in -- in the JNA army. I was extremely struck by the operational zone commander, the divisional commander, by his bearing and his expertise. His subordinates, I got the impression, were not professional soldiers, if I get that correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that was the reason why you said in your statement that because of the non-professionalism of the soldiers themselves, you observed that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have the kind of organisation and discipline that you were accustomed to in an army. Is that your position today as well?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is a difficult question to answer. Based on -- and I'll throw this in as an example: Soon after I arrived in Gornji Vakuf, I came upon a situation in which there was some Italians that had been taken off the route and had been executed. It was an aid convoy. The situation was that I was handed the survivors of that particular incident by the -- by the Muslims in Bugojno. I was -- I suspected at the time that in fact it was a renegade organisation of the Muslims who had actually committed the act. If I use that as a -- as a standpoint or a -- an example, then I would suggest that your statement is correct. There appeared to be dysfunction in that overall structure of who was controlling what organisation. However, whenever I dealt with the leadership, it appeared to be very professional and responsive, and every time I walked into the room, there was a military bearing, to the point where courtesies were awarded to a particular higher echelon of -- of the Muslims every time they entered the room. You knew who was in charge. You knew who was responsible for that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will read out for you now a part of your statement to the Prosecutor. You said: "On the basis of what I have said, it is my opinion that the HVO was better organised, equipped, and structured than the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which I could describe as something more than a group of bandits, hooligans." Could you tell me, what is your view today regarding the organisation and equipment of the HVO and the bulk of the army's forces fighting in your area? I'm not talking about the command structure, whom you have described with precision.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: May I ask: The statement that you refer to that I made, where is that from?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's a statement that you gave on the 9th and 10th of October, 2001 to the Prosecution. And you gave two statements. One had to do with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the other related to the HVO. I have quoted from the first, the former, dealing with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: So in the simplest terms, could you please ask one question that I can respond to. You've got about four or five here that -- I'm not sure where you want to go with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague asked you about the strength of the Armija and the HVO, and I am asking you on the basis of your previous testimony and the testimony you have given today whether when you were present the HVO was better equipped, better organised, and whether its attack force was superior to that of the BH army, whether it was superior in military terms.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The -- I understand where you want to go now. There is a difference between equipment and resources and that of being led professionally. In my opinion, I would say the HVO were better equipped. They appeared to have the tanks. They appeared to have the artillery. They appeared to have new uniforms. To say that they were better led, I'm -- I don't think I can answer that. On the other side, there was an appearance of structure and leadership but not necessarily having all the equipment and the resources to do it. As time progressed, what -- of the battle, what also caught my attention was how different pieces of equipment tended to show up in front of the Armija headquarters every day. Every day we went up there, there was a new piece of equipment that was parked in the front of that headquarters. I would suspect that that was captured equipment from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have clarified the difference between what you previously said and what you have said today before the Trial Chamber. When you said that upon arriving in Bosnia you found out certain things about the situation there, would it be correct to say that you were informed that the conflict between the Armija and the HVO in the area of Prozor had started in October 1992 and continued in January 1993 so that in fact in this area in which the Muslim population accounted for 38 per cent of the population, the majority of that population had already been expelled?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I was well aware of the situation in Prozor when I arrived in -- and was briefed fully on this situation that there had been battles, and even in Gornji Vakuf itself, and the reasons why the population bases were -- were as they were. However, in Prozor there still existed Muslim -- a Muslim community. And more importantly an Imam was in place, which we would do constant visits to in order to establish what the situation was in Prozor, and whether there were any particular problems or anything -- anything that we could help out with. There was a community of women and children that were held in Prozor that were Muslim at the time I was there, even to the point where I personally had visited the camp, the area, which was just off the highway on the left-hand side as you went down to Prozor, to check up on them every now and then. I was briefed fully by the Imam in that location of -- of conditions and how they were being treated and on -- and on and on. I was also informed about battles and problems that had transpired in Prozor and that Prozor for all intents and purposes had become a Croat community.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more question: As you said that on a number of occasions you went to Prozor, the remaining Muslim population was placed in three camps controlled and guarded by the HVO. When you visited them, they were very scared. You were provided with information about maltreatment. And soon after your first visit, they were all expelled from Prozor. Is what I have just said correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: As many -- we thought all of them had been taken, and that was near the end of my tour. There was actually two sets of people in Prozor. There were the women and the children, and then there were the men that were held up at the school. And the Imam was free in the town. In fact, he was only a block and a half from the military police headquarters. The night -- or the day that they had disappeared -- and I say "disappeared" because we didn't know where they -- where they were moved to. We heard all sorts of rumours where they were moved to, but we had just visited this camp with women and children. We walked into the place, and next day we went back to visit and they were gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To go back to the subject of Gornji Vakuf. You said that when you arrived there it was quite clear that intense fighting had been going on for a long time. This was quite visible when one had a look at all the houses there.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That was absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The conflict line passed through the centre of the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: As we were able to determine, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO held elevations above the town and used illegitimate means, because it threw -- it shelled the town with -- with submarine bombs that had been modified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Known as a Livno bomb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Gornji Vakuf was a very important place and before the war the Bosniaks were in the majority there, and at that time the HVO tried to take control of it, as it was an important point leading in the direction of Herzegovina and Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I would say if you say so, because I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this area, given the importance the HVO gave to taking control of this territory, you could quite frequently see additional HVO forces that weren't from Prozor; they had come from Herzegovina. And you could also see parts -- or other parts of the Croatian army engaged in the area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now move on to the subject of Bugojno. And you have already testified about Bugojno in the course of the examination-in-chief. You said that after arriving you had meetings with the HVO and Armija representatives on a number of occasions. But could you also confirm that you had remember meetings with the representatives of the civilian authorities in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I'll make a comment here that I was accused on -- on a couple of occasions of not engaging the civilian hierarchy in -- in discussions. And a couple of times I was stopped on the side of the road by the mayor of Bugojno saying that he wanted to engage more with me on -- in discussions, rather than just the military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning, after your arrival in Bugojno, you were aware of the fact that in the course of 1992 and in 1993 tens of thousands of refugees expelled from Donji Vakuf and from surrounding villages occupied by the Republika Srpska army arrived in Bugojno. Were you aware of this fact, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The staff and part of the HVO brigade - in Bugojno, its name was the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade - were located in the Gorica hill, in the so-called Tito's villa, and that hill was the dominant elevation above the town of Bugojno. Is that fact correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I had visited Tito's lodge on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the HVO and the BH army, as well as the civilian authorities, continually expressed the desire to find a peaceful solution to certain conflicts, and you said that they wanted to continue living together. Nevertheless, you felt that in the month of July the tension started increasing. Would that be a correct description of what you said?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was completely surprised by the -- the turn of events, because on all sides in the town of Bugojno I thought we had full agreement to co-exist as one entity in that town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In June your mission paid particular attention to the protection of humanitarian convoy that consisted of about 500 lorries which advanced in two parts, and the purpose of the convoy was to supply -- provide the town of Tuzla with supplies. This is one of the largest towns in the north-eastern part of Bosnia. Were you particularly engaged in this matter?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that you were provided with UNPROFOR support in Makljen and you were fully engaged in this matter but the military police took away lorries, having threatened you, they maltreated the drivers, and finally, while the convoy was present in your area of responsibility, 36 lorries with their contents were taken from the convoy?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Do you wish me to expand upon that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I would just like you to tell me whether that is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The biggest thing about the Tuzla convoy is the fact that we inherited this convoy. It was neither a United Nations or an ECMM responsibility. This thing was locally organised by the Tuzla, the town of Tuzla, pushed out to Split, and then we started getting reports that this convoy was moving in our direction. We inherited it when it arrived in Prozor, and stepping forward into a very delicate situation was UNPROFOR and ourselves trying to do the best we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In spite of all the efforts that you made, would it be correct to say to say that HVO police in Prozor seized 36 lorries and maltreated the civilians who were with the convoy? You then informed the HVO representatives in Prozor about this fact.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You're aware of the fact that after Prozor, in the territory that you controlled, moved to the area of Travnik and Vitez, you know that there was an organised HVO attack on this convoy and a number of people were killed and over 100 vehicles were -- were seized and were never returned? Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: We witnessed it on TV about two hours after the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this question is being put to you for the sake of my following question: Is it correct to say that such events and such HVO attacks and such an attitude towards the population in Prozor was also one of the reasons for which the misunderstandings and tension in Bugojno itself increased and this was also the subject of discussion at joint meetings?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Because of the particular mission that we were given as the ECMM, we were not out to gather information about military forces. I had an understanding but I did not know specifically in those days the delineation between troops, what corps were involved, and who was doing what to whom, other than what I've described which was Prozor was Croat-controlled, and Gornji Vakuf was joint, and up north was both Croat and Muslim, who eventually became all Muslim. Once again, I was under the understanding that there were three distinct situations in each location, and the other problem was there was an appearance that the boundaries between opposing forces weren't equal. And what I mean by that is the Muslim side to the north didn't necessarily have the same boundaries as those in the south, and a lot of my time was trying to figure out who was up against whom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of June, you were able to see that the HVO, in particular in the area of Makljen and Prozor, had started accumulating heavy equipment; five tanks, two rockets, an M-57, a Howitzer, a 155-millimetre Howitzer, and they started collecting other heavy weapons which you have described in your daily reports. And this in your opinion was proof that the HVO was preparing a large-scale operation. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it was five tanks. I thought it was three tanks, if I remember correctly. And they were being consolidated in the -- the warehouse in Prozor, plus a number of other high-calibre weapons or large-calibre weapons that were being stored down there. I cannot remember whether that was as the operations from the north progressed south or was before the operations that -- that started and it was in fact a response to what was happening in the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be correct to say that at the time you were already aware of the fact that the HVO and the Republika Srpska army were cooperating and you were convinced of this when some of the HVO forces from Bugojno passed through the Serbian territory? They passed through area together with the population that was withdrawing with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The night they disappeared was the first indication that there had been collaboration between the Serbs and the HVO. I was not aware of -- of that ahead of time. We were surprised the fact that 10.000 Croats had moved to the west and then -- and then south into Prozor. It was a shock, because we thought that they were opposing forces at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were on leave in July from the 9th to the 23rd. And as you said, when you returned, the situation had changed completely and dramatically; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, would it be correct to say that with regard to everything I have already asked you about and you yourself directly observed these events - you also observed events after you had returned from your annual leave - you and your colleagues compiled daily reports on all of these events and you recorded who you had spoken to, what you had spoken about, and you recorded the type of activities you engaged in with regard to these events? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were free to draft such reports. You did this on an independent basis. No one pressurised you to include certain facts that you weren't sure of. You weren't -- if you weren't sure that you had actually seen a certain event or heard about it, you wouldn't include it in the report. You were quite free to draft your daily reports.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: The daily reports were a standard format which was used by the ECMM. As a military officer, we tried to place that information in there that was absolutely fact and correct as we had seen it on the ground. We -- inside those reports, we were given the freedom of offering comments into what we thought was up or what we thought the situation was. Otherwise, the stuff that was recorded in there was as we saw it and was fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your reports, you described all the meetings that you had with representatives of the military and civilian authorities and included information about the prisoners in Bugojno, as well as about what you had observed, what you had seen when you visited some of the detention facilities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you returned from leave, you went to Bugojno for the first time on the following day, but on that occasion you didn't attend any meetings. You only saw that the town had been badly damaged as a result of the fighting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: If that's what's written in the report, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the following day - and this is what you said in response to a question from my colleague - you were engaged in an operation in order to transfer the wounded from the HVO as well as the wounded from the Armija. These people were located in the Kalin Hotel.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Are you referring now two days after I returned?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: As I can recollect, that is correct, yes. We went to the Kalin Hotel, and we took out people and then we moved them south. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I will now use a number of dates and facts that are included in your reports, and these reports have already been admitted as evidence by the Chamber. Would it be correct to say that on the 27th of July from the civilian authorities and the chief of the civilian police you asked for permission to gain access to detention facilities in Bugojno because you were informed that they had between 300 and 500 HVO members who were held in detention?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I remember that conversation. If it states so in the report on that date, then yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the following day, you visited the Gimnazija and the furniture showroom. You noticed -- or you made a note of the situation in which the detainees found themselves and you made a note of the number of detainees there. You included this information in your daily report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I believe that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning - and this is not included in your report - you noticed that in these facilities they didn't have the basic essentials, they didn't have enough toilet paper, glasses, soap, and civilian authorities in Bugojno informed you of this and asked you to help them ensure that there were such supplies together with the UNHCR, in order to provide better conditions for the detainees themselves. Was that the subject of your discussion?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I cannot remember specifically whether they offered that or I asked about that information and -- and how that all transpired. All I know is there were stuff that was missing that I had indicated to the -- to the authorities, but I'm not quite sure who -- and I cannot remember honestly whether it was brought up by the -- by the police or by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will adjourn now. It's half past 12.00. We'll have a break and we will resume at five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Defence, I said a moment ago that they had two hours. But very precise calculations that we undertook tell us that you have 1 hour 40. You've already used 30 minutes, so in theory you have 70 minutes left. As we we're working to quarter to 2.00, you have 45 minutes left, and if it is not completed, then we will carry it over to tomorrow, when you will have another half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think I will manage to complete my cross-examination today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, a moment ago we were discussing your visit on the 28th of July to two detention facilities, in the secondary school and in the furniture salon. I would like to check whether I understood you correctly. Is it right that in both facilities it was quite obvious that they were only being temporarily used to house the captives, because there were no suitable facilities for such a large number of prisoners? Is my understanding of the situation correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: To begin with, we did not know the total numbers that were involved, other than what had been told to us, in the neighbourhood of about three to 500, somewhere in there. I didn't know what to expect as to whether it was permanent or not permanent. It appeared that the -- the school or the gym was a facility in which they were holding people. I cannot categorically state that this was a temporary facility at that point in time. What I do remember is after going to the salon, the furniture salon, that called in my mind into question whether this was a permanent facility or not. If I can recollect, it's at that point in time that I am asking the question, is this -- is this where they're staying? And it's a combination of seeing all three of them that I -- I'm getting the information that this is not a permanent facility; hence, whether why they were looking for another facility and eventually they were going to move them to the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can also confirm that the authorities told you that until they move them to the north, all the prisoners would be housed at the Iskra Stadium and in the elementary school and that as of the 5th of August the furniture salon was actually closed.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Without referring to the daily reports, I am not sure when that salon was closed, but I do remember that a consolidation effort was being made and somehow -- I don't remember the elementary school, but I do remember them stating that there might be a consolidation into the sportsplex or to the sports field.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The same day you visited these two facilities where HVO prisoners were held you learnt that in the basement of Tito's Lodge there were 40 imprisoned Muslim civilians and you reported Major -- to Major Binns about this, and you agreed that he should go to Tito's Lodge and that you visit the HVO wounded and try to carry out an exchange. Do you remember these events taking place as I have described them?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But they were not in the basement of Tito's Lodge. They were in a building in front of Tito's Lodge, a hotel, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Major Binns informed you that he was horrified by what he discovered because there were old people in that basement and several children? Actually, you said 22 elderly men and young boys, 14 elderly women, 3 younger ones, and a child, and that they were all mistreated. Do you also remember that Major Binns told you that they were mistreated in the meantime while he left the facility and came back?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Through joint efforts of the ECMM and UNPROFOR, an exchange was carried out of the 23 wounded for the 40 civilians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct. The other thing I would like to make note, it's Major Binns, B-i-n-n-s, who's the name of the company commander of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the HVO, who withdrew from Tito's lodge, which was their last defensive point, and upon withdrawal they set fire to Tito's Lodge?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: That is correct. A clarification: I do not know who set fire to the building. All I know is that once they had left it in fact was burned at night. I'm not sure who lit the match.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answering questions from my learned friend, you said that you met other public figures, particularly Father Janko. Is it true that at the beginning of August you managed to arrange a meeting between Father Janko and representatives of the remaining Croatian population with the head of the civilian police and with the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Can you repeat who the meeting was with? Because there was also at a time where Father Janko was moved to -- down to Prozor and we took the Imam from Prozor up to Gornji Vakuf. Is that -- oh, sorry, up to Bugojno. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. According to your reports, this happened later. But this was at the very beginning. You arranged a meeting attended by Father Janko, the head of the civilian police of Bugojno, representatives of the civilian authorities, and together you discussed the security of the remaining 3.000 Croats left in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that the civilian authorities and the police expressed their complete readiness for the remaining Croat population to join in the authorities and their readiness to take back all the Croats who had left Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I will offer a personal opinion at this time, basically making the statement after a full-fledged operation had just taken place and for civilian authorities to offer Croats back into the town, I would suggest that that offer would not be seen as a legitimate one. Yes, there was talk about it, and I can remember them once again turning and saying, "No, we want to settle things here. We want to allow people back into the community." But I would -- at that time I had a lot of concern to -- to make the statement, "After all this, you still want the people back. And if I was a -- if I was a Croat, would I want to come back."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that early in August the civilian and other authorities in Bugojno also informed you that all the civilians who were temporarily detained during combat operations had been released, that they had been interviewed, and that it had been established that they had no connection with the combat activities, so that 81 captured civilians had been released home?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I do remember them making the statement that some people had been released after interviews, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to show the witness a report which was served on the Defence by the Prosecution during the disclosure procedure so that I might go on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Hauenstein, was this the report referring to the fact you were informed about during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Is this taken directly from my report on that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. This was noted -- it was noted in your report that you were informed about this on the 9th of August, but this is a report we received from the Prosecution and it comes from the competent authorities of Bugojno municipality. My question is merely whether reading this report you can link it to the information you received at the meeting with the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Without seeing my report of that day, I'm unable at this time to put the two -- the two together, because I'm not sure when that exact report was done and exactly what date it was done. If it's around that -- that time frame and those numbers add up, then probably yes. But to look at one document, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be marked for identification only. The Defence could ask the witness to be shown the report from Exhibit 171, but I believe that what the witness has already told us is sufficient regarding the release of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Benjamin, regarding the first document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have the document marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be DH175, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were also informed, as you have already said, that the Iskra Stadium would be transformed into a prisoner -- prison for prisoners of war and that the prisoners would then be detained in only two facilities, and this is also noted in one of your reports; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I cannot recollect that two facilities were going to be used. I remember -- what I remember of -- of the time and of the day was that there were three initial facilities. There was a fourth which we were informed about; we did not know where that was. And then conversation led to that all were going to be moved to a new facility somewhere to the north of Bugojno. I -- I don't remember exactly whether they were being consolidated in the stadium and the school prior to that point. It was a whole bunch of events which led as I was leaving to the point where they were going to all be moved to one location. But it was not the sports field, as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You visited the Iskra Stadium and you can testify that the Iskra Stadium was transformed into a detention facility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I only visited that facility once. It may have been transformed later on after I left, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown the decision of the War Presidency regarding the formation of a provisional detention facility at the Iskra Stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to remind you. You referred to the need for moving the prisoners somewhere north. If I were to remind you, you will see that in Article 1 it says that: "The prisoners should be moved towards the KP Dom Zenica." Does this jog your memory regarding the conversation you had?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: KP Dom Zenica is -- is unfamiliar to me as I sit here today. It may have been referred to at the time. If that is in the direction that I stated which I thought would -- a consolidation was going to take place to the north-east of Bugojno, so Zenica is probably in the neighbourhood, but I cannot specifically remember that name being used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this document, let me ask you: Do you know that the civilian authorities were actually concentrated in the War Presidency, and the mayor was precisely the person that you said met you once in the street and criticised you for not involving him more in the discussions you were having in Bugojno? Was that a civilian body?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: If you're asking me did -- I assumed that the War Presidency was a make-up of military and civilian authorities within Bugojno. Initially when I had arrived there, when we ever -- whenever we tended to meet, we met with both military and civilian in the room at the same time. As aggressions continued in Bugojno, there appeared to be a parting between the civilian and the military structure, and hence why I was a little bit caught flat-footed when I was approached by the -- by the individual standing in the street saying, "Do you know who I am?" It appeared that he was somewhat insulted that I had not consulted him in -- from the point in time that hostilities had commenced.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it -- would I be right in saying and describing the situation by saying that the military commander of the Operative Group West and the military commander of the city of Bugojno were mostly concerned with military affairs and defence lines, whereas all other matters in town were decided by the War Presidency, which also concerned itself with security and other things affecting life in the town of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: In the traditional conduct of military operations, I would say that was a correct statement. Of course I was not privy to the overall structure, and I understood that there was a civilian authority and that there was a military authority, and I would expect that the military authorities were more orientated toward the battlefield as compared to the civilian authority would be more worried about the town of Bugojno itself. I'm unfamiliar with the exact connection between the two and how they ran themselves, other than the joint meetings at the beginning which tended, I felt, to have -- each side tended to part, because depending on their responsibilities, their focus was in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the fact the Defence feels that this is a highly relevant document for this case and the Defence, we would like to suggest that this document be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit, because there's reference to discussions about the Iskra Stadium. It is true that the witness cannot identify the document, but it refers to what he testified about. But in view of the relevance of the document, we would tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn to the Prosecution now. The Defence is asking for the admission into evidence of this order issued by the War Presidency of the Municipality of Bugojno, which is creating a detention centre at the Iskra Stadium to temporarily hold there civilians and the military and that in communication with the KP Dom in Zenica and the military prison in Travnik, once they are -- can function again, they would be moved there. It is also indicated that the centre would be guarded by six civilians and six soldiers. What is the position of the Prosecution? A document that has a stamp and a signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, my friend quite rightly indicated to the Trial Chamber that the witness was not in a position to identify the document, and that is of paramount importance when you want to introduce a document into -- to have the document marked for evidence. And the other reason is that the document before us -- I'm aware of the fact that it has a seal and it appears to be a signature, but our copy - I don't know if it applies to all the other copies - is very, very illegible, especially page 2. The language, it can hardly be seen. And I'm not sure whether that is what is interpreted in the English version. So for those two main reasons, and I think this witness could not in any way shed any light with respect to this document, so I would want to object on those two grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will give it a number and mark it for identification only.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will be DH176, marked for identification for the B/C/S version; and DH176/E, marked for identification for the English translation. I would like to add that the English translation of the report tendered before gets the exhibit number DH175/E, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, is it true to say that as of mid-August representatives of the Croatian people provided you with a list suspecting that 18 crimes had been committed at the expense of Croats, including rapes, robberies, and murder?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: Who provided this list?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Representatives of the Croatian people, as you noted in your report. It could have been Father Janko or someone else representing the Croats.

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I cannot remember specifically receiving such information, and the -- the number that you have given to me, 18, is -- is a number that would not stick in my mind. I do know that at -- at the church where Father Janko was there were lists being amalgamated and brought together of perceived criminal acts that had taken place. I as an ECMM monitor was not in the business of confirming whether these were right or wrong or they were accurate. I was in a position to direct or facilitate the gathering of that information, who would eventually be turned over to the UNHCR or ICRC or others or, in fact, for this Court here today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember a fact that you mentioned in your reports dated the 18th and 19th of August, that what you learnt you passed on to the head of the civilian police, that you requested that he provide you with information and that already the next day the head of the civilian police informed you about the efforts they were making about the fact that two persons had already been taken into custody, that some persons had been taken to court, that some perpetrators are still at liberty, but that -- and also that in two cases it wasn't a crime but that the people were -- died of natural causes? Do you remember this information that was given to you by the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: I remember visiting the chief of police, and I do remember exchanging information. The details that you've just listed to me, I cannot remember specifics about any -- any one -- one event in that list that you've given me. If that is off of a report which I actually wrote, then I would have to state yes. Otherwise, me sitting here today and recollecting a list, I cannot do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My last question is the following: During the numerous conversations that you had with the chief of the civilian police - I could remind you of his name; his name was Senad Dautovic - you were able to see that Dautovic, as the chief of police, was endeavouring to protect the civilian population, to discover the perpetrators, and to take steps against them. To the best of your recollection, is this a correct description of the efforts made to deal with certain problems?

utterances.speaker: PETER HAUENSTEIN
utterances.text: When I met with the chief of police, I found him to be a -- an honourable man. I remember him specifically because we used to exchange a number of stories over where we were from and -- and basically about our families. Whenever I did meet with him, I remember being well taken care of from the point of view that I was always given a cup of coffee and -- and a cigarette. There was always an appearance that he was trying to do the best he could. But because of the situation they were in, that had to be suspect, I believe. For every action of bringing stuff forward that I remember, there was always a counteraction, telling me that yes, okay, we understand what you're trying to bring forward to us but there are -- there is another situation here that we need to have taken a look at. The one thing that I remember specifically is a videotape that had been presented to me for me to make comment on, and it had to do with a bunch of soldiers up in the hills digging up some bodies. And it was presented to me as to -- first of all, to make a statement on behalf of the International Community that something had gone wrong here and, secondly, to make a ruling of some sort. Of course, I backed totally out of that and made no comment and said, "Well, it had to be brought up with the appropriate authorities." It appeared there -- there were things in order. But to make a statement that -- that there was something behind it, I can't tell you sitting here today. I remember fondly sitting there discussing issues with the gentleman, but -- but that's as far as I can take it, unless you want any more information other than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that completes my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, there'll be no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I feared that you would have to testify tomorrow too, but thanks to the wisdom of the Defence who put very concise questions to you, we have completed your examination. I would like to thank you for having come here to testify. You have answered questions put to you by both parties. And I wish you a good trip home. And naturally, I wish you all the best for the mission that you are currently engaged in. I would now like to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The schedule was adhered to. And before I give Mr. Withopf the floor, as far as the schedule for tomorrow is concerned, perhaps Mr. Withopf could tell us something about that, as well as bidding us farewell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours. In respect to the schedule for tomorrow, the witness whose name appears on the confidential witness schedule is in town and he can be made available to testify tomorrow. Otherwise, Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm not intending to hold a long speech. However, due to the fact that I'm the last time in court today before this Trial Chamber, I wish to thank. I wish to thank first and foremost my team, not only the team members who appeared before this Tribunal but also and in particular to those team members, both the legal and the investigation team, who are working behind the scenes and quite often under quite adverse circumstances. I wish also to thank everybody in and around the courtroom who are facilitating our work, such as the usher, the translators, the technicians, the court reporter, and the security personnel. I think their contribution to a smooth running of the proceedings can't be overestimated, and I think we quite often intend to forget the importance of their work. Of course, I wish to thank all the representatives of the registrar, who for obvious reasons have a very important and a crucial role in these proceedings, as do have the Chamber's legal officers obviously, who are for both parties the necessary link to the Trial Chamber. In respect to more practical issues of a more administrative nature, I wish to thank them as well. I wish to thank Defence counsel, all Defence counsel and all assistants to Defence counsel. I think it became apparent -- I think it became very apparent in the course of these proceedings that despite all heated debates from time to time, heated debates, the Prosecution and all members of the Defence team had a good working relationship, if not to say an exceptionally good work relationship. This good working relationship certainly ensured the fact that this trial has, in our view, run quite smoothly over the last month and this good relationship has also ensured, in our view, the maintenance of the quite exceptional pace of these proceedings. Finally, Mr. President, Your Honours, I hope that I was able to contribute to the very difficult task of the Trial Chamber, of the Chamber, your Honourable Judges, to find out the truth in this case. On a last note, I wish to -- everybody -- I wish everybody in and around the courtroom all the best for their professional but more importantly for their private life. Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Is there anything that Defence counsel would like to say? Yes, Mrs. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of my colleagues from the Kubura team and from General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team, we would just like to confirm everything that my learned colleague has just said. We have worked in a professional situation, and thanks to Mr. Withopf in particular we have managed to fulfil our duties as Defence counsel. In such a situation, it is difficult for the Defence to only speak positively about the role of the Prosecutor. We won't speak about this at the moment because, as my colleague has said, we have often been in conflict with the Prosecution and often we have had quite significant requests which were addressed to the Prosecution. That is our role. That is our role, because as Defence counsel we have to fight to prove our client's cases. But in order to proceed, it is necessary to have good -- a good working relationship with the Prosecution. Thanks to Mr. Withopf, I would like to say that both teams were very happy with our collaboration, and we would like to wish him all the best in his new position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would the other Defence team like to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could add to what my learned friend has said in thanking Mr. Withopf for everything that he has done in contributing to the effective functioning of this trial and the professional manner in which it has been conducted. It has been a joy and a pleasure to work with him, and I do on behalf of everyone wish him very well in his new position at the ICC, and I'm sure he will contribute greatly to bringing the first cases and first indictments before that historic court. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. The Trial Chamber naturally wishes you all the best in your future career in ICC. We were very glad to see that when the Trial Chamber requested that you provide them with tables or other documents, you were always able to comply with our requests, and in the course of the debates before the Chamber you always responded very courteously to the requests made by the Judges or to the comments expressed by the Defence. We wish you all the best in your career and perhaps in some other life we will meet you again. It's almost 1.45 now. We haven't worked beyond this time. I would like to thank everyone present, and I would like to invite everyone to appear tomorrow at 9.00, without Mr. Withopf, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
